Guns In The Sky [6268]

By: Hein Kaiser | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
we find the black hole where guns in the care of SAPS may be disappearing into.

Unique Selling Point:
Guns seem to go missing in the SAPS all the time, and even Police Minister Bheki Cele admitted to this. But it seems nothing is being done about it and a major loophole in the manual administration process of guns means it could happen indefinitely, without detection except in hindsight, until the loophole is closed.

Summary:
There is an administrative loophole that contributes significantly to the massive theft or disappearance of firearms from police custody. We expose this loophole and peel back the layers that expose dangerous SAPS incompetence when it comes to managing firearms. We use 2 case studies, the Norwood Police Station where stolen guns ended up in criminal activity and in Pretoria, where confiscated guns in an illegal raid ended up in retail.

Further information:
By his own admission, Police Minister Beheki Cele said in March that 7 331 firearms and 10 million rounds of ammo stolen or lost over 10 years were lost by the SAPS. And after investigating this story, it’s not hard to believe.
Earlier this year 158 guns were stolen from Norwood police station and the officer in charge committed suicide. Last year, guns stolen from the same police station were recovered after a heist in Brakpan. The 13Store, where police store guns and evidence, is said to be in a mess.
But its not the only police station to lose guns. And it was not Norwood’s first rodeo with stolen guns. It is endemic throughout the SAPS and the biggest problem are the paperwork loopholes and SOPs not being followed that create the perfect porous environment.

And Jenni Irish-Qhobosheane of the World Organisation Against Organised Crime knows exactly where the guns go, and how they get there. She authored two research papers that evidence the flaws, the missing links and how guns handed in for amnesty, even saps issued guns and confiscated firearms are mishandled and traded by the police.

And much to his own frustration, gun dealer Christoph Roelofse has first hand experience of police ineptitude when it comes to losing guns. 528 of his guns are missing, and some of them ended up in retail again….

In short, receiving guns into evidence requires pen and paperwork. It’s the only area in the entire SAPS value chain that is not digital. And it can be exploited, easily. Nobody is following the rules, and that is how guns end up back on the streets, get resold or just go missing. Jenni’s report says this, too.

Guns Edit 002 - 28 November.mp4

VO: [00:00:05]
Violent crime is our daily curse in South Africa. And it’s getting worse.
Every year, more than 9000 guns are reported stolen or missing, and around 8000 guns are traded illegally in South Africa. It's a scary number and can explain why almost 30 people are shot and killed in our country every day. There is nothing as frightening as staring down the barrel of a criminal's gun and nothing as disturbing as finding out that it came from a police evidence room.

SIMON VOX POP: About a year and a half ago, we were hijacked. But outside this complex here, we drove in over here. We arrived at this little intercom machine over here. A guy came out of the bush up with a gun in the accident. A shot went off, and my driver just put the controversy and reversed over up the road till over the speed hump when the car stalled. And that's when I realized that he had been injured. We discovered was the bullet which was found in the car was a full metal jacket, which was a police issue.

VO: Thousands of illegal firearms flood the streets every year. Recently, Police Minister Bheki Cele admitted that many of these weapons come from police stations like this one. But how does that even happen?

VO: [00:01:41] A report in March this year revealed that seven 331 firearms and 10 million rounds of ammunition was either stolen or lost by the police in the past decade. But that's what we know of. It's estimated that there are around two and a half million illicit firearms doing the rounds in South Africa. But nobody really knows for sure.

JENNI: [00:02:05] We can't actually say how many firearms are going missing from SAPS 13 stores, evidence stores, armories. But evidence suggests that it is significant.

VO: [00:02:16] These evidence stores are called 13 stores, and inside them there are arms seized from criminals and guns handed in by licensed gun owners during amnesty or when a gun is no longer needed by its owner. Jenny Irish Quoboshiane has spent 20 years researching organized crime for several organizations, including The police. Right now, she is a researcher at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime and the author of several reports that provide frightening insight into the state of firearms control in South Africa.

JENNI: [00:02:52] I think our firearms control is not working. It's dysfunctional. Historically, a lot of our firearms came across the borders and from conflict zones. But more and more, we're seeing firearms coming into the illicit firearm market from domestic sources. And having a dysfunctional firearms control system is obviously contributing to that.

VO: At Last count, the state owns around 1.3 million firearms, and more than half of these are owned by the military and the SAPS. The rest are with Correctional Services and other government agencies. It amounts to a potentially unlimited supply of deadly weapons. And the numbers just keep climbing.

UPSOUND CHRISTOPHER: So now they have the keys for the safe room. Right.

VO: Christopher Roelofse has been somewhat of a celebrity in the firearms and hunting world for 25 years. He runs his own blog and is frequently called upon as an expert by specialist media. In 2019, he decided to open his own specialist firearms store on a smallholding in eastern Pretoria. At the time he probably couldn’t imagine the dark days that lay ahead of him.

CHRISTOPHER: The moment when the building was completed, of course, we moved the dealership, moved stock to the facility. And on the day that we are informed we are no longer welcome on the land. As a matter of fact we got locked out.
MASA: And why is that?
CHRISTOPER: That is a total mystery.
VO: Christopher’s nightmare was about to unfold.




CHRISTOPHER: A captain beeep. Inform me that I need to come out to the facility immediately and made various accusations regarding illegal firearms and was very imminent in the fact that I'm going to be arrested.

VO: The police shut him down before he could open his doors because his landlord and business partner accused him of having illegal guns.


CHRISTOPHER: I inquired about a search warrant. I was informed that if they wanted a search warrant, they could get it in no time.

VO: [00:05:00] The police took all the firearms away in an unmarked vehicle and according to CHristoper, it was his landlord’s delivery bakkie that carried the haul. They carted everything away, including Christopher's paperwork that kept detail of each of the weapons in stock.

CHRISTOPHER: We provided them with all the registers so they could check the firearms against the registries. They refused to do that. EVerytime when I questioned anything, I was threatened with arrest.

LINK: We've all heard stories of the police being weaponised before, and this may be one of those scenarios, but it gets worse. The firearms that were confiscated from here, all 528 of them have gone missing in action too.

VO: The firearms were supposed to be taken to a police station down the road. But Christophe said that they never arrived and there's no paper trail for any of this.

MASA: How do we find ourselves in this kind of position where the state is losing firearms, SAPS is losing firearms out of evidence rooms?

JENNI: State entities and state government departments are supposed to follow certain procedures, and that just isn't happening.

VO: [00:06:07] When firearms are seized or handed into a police station, they're supposed to be now sent to and tested by forensics if needs be, and then onto a central provincial armory as soon as possible. It's still a manual process, despite more than 300 million Rand that was spent on developing an electronic process almost ten years ago that has never been switched on fully. Managing firearms at SAPS starts on paper, and that's how sometimes just like case dockets, they may disappear.

VO: We visited a gun dealership in Witbank where owner Andrew Souton and Jonathan Fouche, the chairperson of the SA Gundealers Association, showed me around the collection of historical firearms.

UPSOUND MASA - AK47

VOl Both Andrew and Jonathan reached the end of their patience with the antiquated system the police still use to manage dangerous weapons.

JONATHAN: Creates a myriad of loopholes. So many, in fact, that it's like a sieve. Anybody who wants to create illegal firearms to give firearms to the criminal element can do so with a very low probability of it ever being detected.

VO: Frustration drove them to take the police to court simply to force them to just do their job, to build an electronic system that instantly synchronizes dealer stock with the police register. Right now, there can be a six month period where the data between dealer and the police is completely out of sync. And in that time period, anything can happen.


JONATHAN: [00:07:19] Because the police process firearms on a transactional basis. They record any movement at any point in time, but it's not time stamped. which is why dealers end up having a big mismatch between the real stock on their premises and what the police think a dealer would have.

VO: A time stamp is almost like a digital signature that cannot be changed. A manual process could be abused. And after three years, Christopher is still looking for his paperwork.

CHRISTOPHER: Once those firearms arrive at the police station, they need to be properly entered into a general 13th register. And over and above that, you are supposed to issue a receipt according to the law, and then they need to be entered into it sapsa dfo register and then needs to be reported to provincial DEA folks. In other words, the province is now informed that they all firearms at that police station and they are supposed to inspect it on a regular basis. Of course, none of this happened for three years.

VO: [00:08:36] And he is still looking for his firearms.

VO: While we were filming at the place where Christopher last saw his guns, the man allegedly behind it all, his landlord, arrived.

MASA: [00:46:31] Terms of this guy. Hi there. We're filming an interview with Christopher, and we are filming an interview with Christopher. Yeah. Because we're doing a story with Christopher about his firearms.
MASA: It was illegal?
MASA:] No. He says your firearms were here illegally.

CHRISTOPHER: That's what he says.

MASA: Good. Thank you. We may continue now. I assume you know that gentleman.

CHRISTOPHER: [00:47:10] Now, that's the ex partner, the idiot. Sorry, folks.

VO: We expected an argument, but the landlord said what he wanted to say and then, retreated.


VO: [00:08:43] In the three years that Christopher has been looking for his guns, about 15 police stations were robbed of their weapons around the country while others simply lost arms in their posession. Norwood police station in Johannesburg gained notoriety for this, firearms are not safe here.

LINK: In 2014, an entire cache was discovered at a house nearby the police station, and in 2021, more guns went missing from its armory, the infamous SAPS 13 store.

VO: [00:09:14] When police raided the house down the road from the Norwood police station eight years ago. They discovered 300 firearms. Since then, no light has been shed on what happened, despite an investigation.

JENNI: [00:09:29] The case seems to have just fizzled out. We don't know what happened to those firearms.

VO: [00:09:34] And, astonishingly, just last year 178 firearms went missing from the station's 13 store, too, upping the area's illicit gun tally significantly.

MASA: [00:09:43] So how are these guns made to disappear?

JENNI: [00:09:46] People would have to have access to what else supposed to be highly secured. SAPS 13 stores either with people not bothering to ask any questions or with people complicit in those firearms moving out.

VO: [00:09:59] We approached the police for comment, but after being sent from provincial spokesperson to national and then back again, the police were looking for a subject matter expert to answer our questions. We are still waiting.

SIMON VOX POP: [00:11:24] It's beyond comprehension that criminals can actually get hold of ammunition that's been issued to the police. If you want to buy liquor, you go to a liquor shop. If you want to buy ammunition, you go to a cop shop.

But its not the only police station to lose guns. And it was not Norwood’s first rodeo with stolen guns. It is endemic throughout the SAPS and the biggest problem are the paperwork loopholes and SOPs not being followed that create the perfect porous environment. And Jenni Irish-Qhobosheane of the World Organisation Against Organised Crime knows exactly where the guns go, and how they get there. She authored two research papers that evidence the flaws, the missing links and how guns handed in for amnesty, even saps issued guns and confiscated firearms are mishandled and traded by the police. And much to his own frustration, gun dealer Christoph Roelofse has first hand experience of police ineptitude when it comes to losing guns. 528 of his guns are missing, and some of them ended up in retail again…. In short, receiving guns into evidence requires pen and paperwork. It’s the only area in the entire SAPS value chain that is not digital. And it can be exploited, easily. Nobody is following the rules, and that is how guns end up back on the streets, get resold or just go missing. Jenni’s report says this, too.
